title: Bootstrap tests of the 2016-2026 ASASSN-14ko clock reject steady decay and a cubic; an on-off decay beats 0.6-d-per-orbit period kicks only at p = 0.025-0.05 if the half-rise lag is constant
abstract: Question: the repeating nuclear transient ASASSN-14ko had a fast period decrease before 2020 and a constant period in the 2020-2024 X-ray clock. Is this stall a chance quiet phase of random period kicks, a smooth change of the decay rate, or an on-off switch of the decay? Peak times cannot answer this, because peaks have shape-dependent delays. Approach: we reduced the 163 public NICER observations without HEASoft and fitted box-dip ingress times jointly with Swift XRT; we also used the independent deep-suppression times of SCI 2b5fd32c. We measured the lags of the optical half-rise and the UV peak after the X-ray dip, used the half-rise (14 cycles, 2016-2026) as a pericentre proxy, and compared five clock models with AIC and two-sided parametric bootstraps. Results: the half-rise follows the deep suppression by 4.67 +/- 0.54 d (chi2 1.4 for 3 dof; extra scatter below 1.3 d) and our box ingress by 5.75 +/- 0.54 d; the UV-peak lag to the box ingress varies by 5.9 d. Our 2021 box ingresses are 0.8-3.5 d before the deep suppression. Inside 2020-2024 the published Pdot = -0.0026 is rejected (delta chi2 11-53 for 0-1 d jitter). Over 2016-2026, AIC prefers an on-off clock (constant period for 7-13 orbits from about cycle 21, Pdot about -0.004 before; AIC 73.8) to a cubic (85.1), stationary kicks of 0.59 d per orbit (94.5) and constant Pdot (107.5). Bootstraps reject constant Pdot (p < 1/150) and the cubic (p < 1/60 under the cubic), but favour the on-off clock over stationary kicks only at p = 0.05 (fixed breaks) and 0.025 (break search); the data are also less clean than a pure on-off clock predicts (p < 1/60). Kicks need 0.4-1.0 d per orbit for the long record but less than 0.4 d per orbit inside the X-ray era; an era-dependent kick size is not detected (p = 0.54). Forecasts for the flares of 2026 November and 2027 February differ by 7-10 d. Limitations: we assume that the half-rise lag outside 2020-2024 equals the lag measured in four cycles; the post-stall decrease rests on three half-rise times; breaks and markers were chosen after inspection; bootstraps are small (40-200 samples); no public data cover the 2026 flares.

display.caption: X-ray deep-suppression times and optical half-rise times (offset removed) relative to the linear X-ray clock, with five clock models fitted to all points; bottom: implied period per cycle. AIC prefers the on-off model E, but bootstraps favour it over stationary kicks K only at p = 0.025-0.05.

Left: box-ingress (this work) and deep-suppression X-ray markers of 2020-2024 against the linear clock; dotted: fit with Pdot fixed at -0.0026. Right: the optical half-rise keeps a constant lag after both X-ray markers; the UV-peak lag is constant only for deep suppression.

NICER (top), Swift XRT (middle) and UVOT UVW2 (bottom) light curves of the 2021 cycles 22-24 with the joint box-dip fit. The box ingress (blue) comes before the linear clock (dotted); green dashed: optical half-rise; magenta: UVW2 peak.

citations.reason: We use its deep-suppression X-ray markers as primary clock markers. Our independent NICER box fits confirm its early, slow 2021 dip onsets.
We use its Swift XRT counts, reference times, UVW2 markers and box-dip model, and extend its X-ray clock to 2016-2026 with a pericentre proxy.
We use its optical half-rise times and Swift UVOT light curve.
Its random period kicks of about 0.6 d per orbit fit our pericentre-proxy clock and are not rejected by calibrated bootstraps (p = 0.025-0.05 against an on-off decay).
Its period-noise evidence agrees in size with our long-span kick fit; inside the X-ray era the kicks must be smaller.
It asked for a pericentre marker to separate kicks from emission delays; we supply an X-ray-tied half-rise marker and do this test.
Its low power from future peaks motivates our use of a lag-calibrated marker instead of peaks.
Its precessing star-disc drag is an on-off clock of the type that AIC prefers; our bootstraps favour this type only weakly.
Delay changes that it allows are limited to about 1 d for the half-rise lag in 2020-2024.
We address its marker-offset problem with lags measured against one X-ray marker.
Its constant period near 108 d after 2020 agrees with the stall phase of our clock.
Its SPHEREx peak is a peak marker; we did not use it in the fits.
Its failure of an energy-proportional period change agrees with an on-off clock.
